# Correlation Is Not Causation {#sec-causation}

```{python}
#| label: ch13-setup
import textwrap

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scripts import water as w
from scripts.figures import INK, style
from scripts.prose import number_words, spans, text_holds

A = w.A
res = w.res()
k = res["k"]
names, colors = w.names(), w.colors()
kind = {c: n.rsplit(", ", 1)[0] for c, n in names.items()}
rho = res["irca_infant"].set_index("cluster")
bins = res["irca_infant_bins"]
bins = bins[bins["n"] >= 20]
rho_lo, rho_hi = rho["spearman_rho"].min(), rho["spearman_rho"].max()
pooled_rho = rho["all_clusters_rho"].iloc[0]
pooled_n = int(rho["all_clusters_n"].iloc[0])


def sgn(x):
    return f"{x:+.2f}".replace("-", "−")
```

```{python}
#| label: ch13-checks
# Values for the prose, and guards for its sentences whose words depend on the data.
NUM = number_words(zero="no")


IM_YEARS = spans(A.OUTCOME_YEARS["infant_mortality"])
text_holds(IM_YEARS == "2017–2019 and 2021–2023", "the years in fig-wat-within's caption")
c_lo, c_hi = int(rho["spearman_rho"].idxmin()), int(rho["spearman_rho"].idxmax())
text_holds(pooled_rho > 0 and rho["spearman_rho"].abs().max() < 0.2
           and abs(rho_hi - pooled_rho) < 0.01, "weak associations, one as large as the pooled one")
silhouette = res["summary"]["silhouette_at_k"]
cl = res["clusters"]
zsd = cl.groupby("cluster")[["z_ipm", "z_rural_share", "z_water_coverage", "z_altitude_m"]].std()
text_holds((zsd < 1).all().all() and silhouette < 0.3, "places more alike within clusters, far from equal")

# The check's units, as irca_vs_infant() builds them: one municipality-year, the unweighted mean
# IRCA of its scored zones (in the cluster, or over all of them for the pooled figure).
rows = cl[cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].dropna(subset=["infant_mortality"])
units = rows.groupby(["cluster", "divipola", "year"])["irca"].mean()
pooled_units = rows.groupby(["divipola", "year"]).agg(irca=("irca", "mean"), zones=("zone", "nunique"))
text_holds(len(pooled_units) == pooled_n, "the pooled units")
one_zone = (pooled_units["zones"] == 1).mean()
# Range restriction: the clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so it varies less inside some of them.
sd_all = pooled_units["irca"].std()
sd_c = units.groupby(level="cluster").std()
narrow, wide = [int(c) for c in sd_c.index if sd_c[c] < sd_all], [int(c) for c in sd_c.index if sd_c[c] >= sd_all]
text_holds(narrow and wide and (rho.loc[wide, "spearman_rho"].abs() < abs(pooled_rho)).all(),
           "IRCA's spread within the clusters")

# Blank rates: the series has no zeros, so a blank may be a recorded zero.
my = cl[cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].drop_duplicates(["divipola", "year"])
blank = my["infant_mortality"].isna().mean()
pop = w.raw().groupby(["divipola", "year"])["population"].sum()
my_pop = my.join(pop.rename("muni_pop"), on=["divipola", "year"])
text_holds(w.raw()["infant_mortality"].eq(0).sum() == 0
           and my_pop.loc[my_pop["infant_mortality"].isna(), "muni_pop"].median()
           < my_pop.loc[my_pop["infant_mortality"].notna(), "muni_pop"].median(),
           "a series without zeros, blank in smaller places")


def clusters_text(cs):
    return f"cluster {cs[0]}" if len(cs) == 1 else "clusters " + ", ".join(map(str, cs[:-1])) + f" and {cs[-1]}"


def sds_text(cs):
    return " and ".join(f"{sd_c[c]:.1f}" for c in cs)


# fig-wat-within's alt text: how far the band medians move within a cluster.
band_move = bins.groupby("cluster")["median"].agg(lambda m: m.max() - m.min()).max()
text_holds(f"{band_move:.1f}" == "3.1" and sgn(rho_lo) == "−0.04" and sgn(rho_hi) == "+0.10",
           "fig-wat-within's alt text")

# Tunja (@sec-tunja-kind) in this check: one municipality-year, the mean IRCA of its zones.
tj = cl[(cl["divipola"] == "15001") & cl["year"].isin(A.INFANT_YEARS)].dropna(subset=["infant_mortality"])
tj_c = int(tj["cluster"].iloc[0])
tj_mean = tj.groupby("year")["irca"].mean()
tj_u = tj[tj["zone"] == "urban"].set_index("year")["irca"]
tj_r = tj[tj["zone"] == "rural"].set_index("year")["irca"]
tj_share = tj["rural_share"].max()
tj_yr = int((tj_r - tj_u).idxmax())             # the year its zones' water differed most
text_holds(tj["municipio"].eq("TUNJA").all() and tj["cluster"].eq(tj_c).all()
           and list(tj_u.index) == list(tj_r.index) == list(tj_mean.index) and (tj_u < tj_r).all(),
           "Tunja's averaged zones")
```

The analysis was built to ask whether places with worse water have worse outcomes, and the
temptation, once there is a chart, is to read the answer as an effect: worse water causes more
infant deaths. The data cannot support that sentence, and this chapter shows why, with the
analysis's own numbers.

One more comparison, the association between water safety and infant mortality *within* each kind
of place, comes out weak in every kind, and in one as large as across all of them. But neither a
strong association nor a weak one could settle the causal question here, and the reasons decide how the results must be written.
That last part is not a formality: the sentence a reader quotes is the one you publish.

## Worse water, more infant deaths? {#sec-water-within}

Across all municipality-years with both values in `{python} IM_YEARS`, the rank correlation
between utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality is `{python} sgn(pooled_rho)` (n =
`{python} w.fmt(pooled_n)`). *Spearman's* $\rho$ (rho) measures whether two variables rise and fall
together in rank order, from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 (no monotonic relation) to +1
(perfectly together), and it is not thrown by extreme values, which matters with small municipalities'
noisy rates.

A small positive association across all places could come from water, or from everything that
differs between places with safe and unsafe water. The clusters offer a partial control: within a
cluster, places are more alike in poverty, rurality, coverage and altitude than across the country,
though far from equal (the silhouette in @sec-choose-k was `{python} f"{silhouette:.2f}"`). So the check
repeats the comparison inside each cluster (@fig-wat-within).

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-within
#| fig-cap: "Median infant mortality by utility-supplied IRCA band, within each cluster; 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 pooled. Bands with fewer than 20 municipality-years are not drawn. Descriptive only: not a causal effect of water safety."
#| fig-alt: "Four small panels, one per cluster, each titled with the cluster's number and kind. Each shows median infant mortality across the IRCA risk bands, labelled N, L, M, H and U for no risk, low, medium, high and unfit. Within any cluster the medians differ across the bands by at most 3.1 per 1,000, and the Spearman correlations printed on the panels lie between −0.04 and +0.10."
#| classes: on-light
with style():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, k, figsize=(7.2, 2.9), sharey=True)
    for ax, (c, g) in zip(axes, bins.groupby("cluster")):
        pos = [A.IRCA_BANDS.index(b) for b in g["irca_band"]]
        ax.plot(pos, g["median"], marker=A.CLUSTER_MARKERS[c - 1], ms=5, color=colors[c])
        ax.set_title(textwrap.fill(f"{c} · {kind[c]}", 16, break_on_hyphens=False), fontsize=8,
                     loc="left", fontweight="bold", color=colors[c])
        ax.text(0.05, 0.06, f"ρ = {sgn(rho.loc[c, 'spearman_rho'])}\nn = {rho.loc[c, 'n']:,}",
                transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8, color=INK)
        ax.set_xticks(range(5), ["N", "L", "M", "H", "U"], fontsize=8)
        ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=8)
    axes[0].set_ylim(0, bins["median"].max() * 1.3)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("Infant mortality\nper 1,000", fontsize=8)
    fig.supxlabel("IRCA band: N no risk · L low · M medium · H high · U unfit", fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

Within the clusters, $\rho$ runs from `{python} sgn(rho_lo)` in cluster `{python} c_lo` to
`{python} sgn(rho_hi)` in cluster `{python} c_hi`, where it is as large as across all places. Two things
make these figures hard to set beside the pooled one. The clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so inside
`{python} clusters_text(narrow)` it varies less: standard deviations of `{python} sds_text(narrow)`
against `{python} f"{sd_all:.1f}"` across all places, and a narrower range weakens a rank correlation by
construction. (In `{python} clusters_text(wide)` it varies more, `{python} sds_text(wide)`, and $\rho$ is
weaker there too.) And the units differ, because the unit follows the outcome. Infant mortality is
measured for a whole municipality, so each municipality-year counts once, with the mean IRCA of its zones:
all of them for the pooled figure, only those in the cluster for a cluster's.

That mean is unweighted, and it covers only the zones with a score: in
`{python} f"{one_zone:.0%}"` of the pooled municipality-years only one zone has one. So the IRCA beside a
rate is one zone's score or the plain mean of two, not what the average resident drinks.

It would be easy to read this as "water does not matter". That reading is as unsupported as the first one.

## What else could explain it {#sec-confounders}

@fig-confounders draws the paths between water and infant mortality that the data cannot separate.

![What else could explain it. The dashed arrow is the question; every other path can create an association without an effect, or hide an effect that exists.](../media/diagrams/confounders){#fig-confounders .on-light fig-alt="The question is whether unsafe water raises infant mortality, a dashed arrow from water safety to infant deaths. Other paths connect the two. Poverty and rurality make water less safe and also make infant deaths more likely, a confounder. Poverty also limits health-service access, which affects infant deaths. Reporting quality stands between real and recorded deaths: weak registration hides deaths. And IRCA is measured per zone while infant deaths are per municipality."}

**Poverty and rurality** are likely *confounders*: poorer, more rural places tend to have less safe water
and, for other reasons, more infant deaths. They can produce an association between water and mortality
with no effect of water at all.
**Health-service access**, worse in poor and remote places, lies on another path to infant deaths.
**Reporting quality** works the other way: places with weak birth and death registration record fewer
infant deaths than occur, and if those are also the places with unsafe water, under-recording can *hide* a
real effect. Blanks add a second problem. The series holds no zeros, so a blank rate may mean no deaths
were recorded, and `{python} f"{blank:.0%}"` of the clustered municipality-years in these years are blank.
Leaving them out drops what may be recorded zeros, which raises small places' averages most: a selection
on the outcome itself.

Then there is the **ecological level**. IRCA is measured for an urban or rural zone, infant mortality for
the whole municipality. A pattern across places need not hold for the people in them: the infants who
died need not be the ones drinking the worst water. Drawing individual conclusions from aggregate data is
known as the *ecological fallacy*.

Tunja shows the mismatch in one place. In this check each of its `{python} NUM[len(tj_mean)]`
municipality-years counts once in cluster `{python} tj_c`, with the mean IRCA of its two zones: in
`{python} tj_yr`, for example, `{python} f"{tj_mean[tj_yr]:.2f}"`, halfway between its urban water's
`{python} f"{tj_u[tj_yr]:.1f}"` and its rural water's `{python} f"{tj_r[tj_yr]:.1f}"`, a value neither zone
had. The mean weighs the two zones equally, though at most `{python} f"{tj_share:.0%}"` of Tunja's people
live in the rural one, and the infant mortality beside it is the whole municipality's.

The clusters narrow some of these differences without removing them: within a cluster, places still
differ in poverty and access. And small municipalities produce extreme rates, which add noise that flattens any line.

::: practice
**Pause and think.** Pick one of these. Could it hide a real effect, or create a fake one?

Poverty can create a fake one: if poorer places tend to have both less safe water and, for other reasons,
more infant deaths, the two move together without water doing anything. Reporting quality can hide a real one: if unsafe-water places under-record deaths, their
measured rates are too low, and a real effect looks smaller than it is. Most confounders can push either
way, which is exactly why a correlation cannot settle the question.
:::

A causal claim needs a design that handles these paths, not a better chart: for example, comparing places
before and after a change in water treatment, against comparable places without the change. That is a
different study, with different data.

## Writing it honestly {#sec-honest-writing}

Every output of this analysis says the same thing in the same words, because the project's rules require
it: comparisons between clusters are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of water safety.
In practice that means a few habits:

- Describe what was compared, and over which rows: "within each cluster, `{python} IM_YEARS`,
  municipality-years with both values".
- Use verbs of association ("is higher in", "varies with"), not of effect ("raises", "reduces", "leads
  to").
- Name the data's limits beside the result: the utility-supplied IRCA, the method change in infant
  mortality, the zone-versus-municipality mismatch.
- State what the result does *not* show, in one sentence a reader could quote.

::: pitfall
The causal sentence usually arrives in the last step: a slide title, a blog post's headline, a summary
for a council. Ask the assistant to check every title and summary against the project's rules, and read
them yourself. "Utility-supplied water risk (IRCA) and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities" is a fair title; "How
unsafe water kills infants" is not, however strongly you suspect it.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

Across all places, IRCA and infant mortality are weakly associated (Spearman's $\rho$ =
`{python} sgn(pooled_rho)`); within the clusters it runs from `{python} sgn(rho_lo)` to
`{python} sgn(rho_hi)`, as large as the pooled figure in one, and narrowed partly by design, since the
clusters were formed partly on IRCA. Neither number shows an effect, or its absence. Poverty
and rurality can create an association, health-service access lies on another path, weak reporting can
hide deaths, blanks may be recorded zeros, and the data meet at different levels, as Tunja's averaged zones show. A causal claim needs
a design that deals with these, such as before-and-after comparisons with comparable places. Until then,
write about association, over named rows, with the limits beside the result, and check every title and
summary against that rule before it goes out. @sec-publish-many takes the results, and those sentences,
to the officials and the council, in every format they need.

- W. S. Robinson, "Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals", *American Sociological Review*
  15(3), 351–357 (1950), doi:[10.2307/2087176](https://doi.org/10.2307/2087176), the classic account of the
  ecological fallacy; cited, with the Spearman paper, in `examples/water/references.bib`, checked against
  their publishers' pages (2026-11-01; pages from the paper's 2009 reprint in the *International Journal of
  Epidemiology*, checked 2026-11-12).
- Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, [*Causal Inference: What If*](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook)
  (Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2020; free online), on confounding and designs for causal questions (checked 2026-11-12).
- SciPy, [`spearmanr`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.spearmanr.html),
  the rank correlation and its assumptions (checked 2026-11-12).
